items.title: 4.1.5.2 How We Traverse a Tree Using BFS?

source_refs.note: Topic 4.1.5.2 How We Traverse a Tree Using BFS (PDF 103-104, printed 100-101), as printed: Figure 4.4 and the 17 numbered steps (sub-points joined into their step).

blocks.text: Breadth-First Search (BFS) is an algorithm used to explore and traverse tree structures by visiting nodes level by level. This approach uses a queue to manage the nodes that need to be visited. Below is a detailed explanation using a numeric tree example. The figure 4.4 illustrates the tree structure used in our BFS example:

blocks.alt: Binary tree of seven light green nodes: 1 at the top; 2 and 3 below it; 4 and 5 under 2; 6 and 7 under 3.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.4: Balanced Binary Tree (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.4).

items: Start at the Root: Begin at the root node (1). This node is placed into the queue.
Visit Node 1: Dequeue node 1 and visit it. Add its children (nodes 2 and 3) to the queue.
Visit Node 2: Dequeue node 2 and visit it. Add its children (nodes 4 and 5) to the queue.
Visit Node 3: Dequeue node 3 and visit it. Add its children (nodes 6 and 7) to the queue.
Visit Node 4: Dequeue node 4 and visit it. Node 4 has no children, so the queue remains unchanged.
Visit Node 5: Dequeue node 5 and visit it. Node 5 has no children, so the queue remains unchanged.
Visit Node 6: Dequeue node 6 and visit it. Node 6 has no children, so the queue remains unchanged.
Visit Node 7: Dequeue node 7 and visit it. Node 7 has no children, so the queue is now empty.
Completion: The queue is empty, indicating that all nodes have been visited in a level-by-level order.
